# Writing statistical results

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- write matched methods and results paragraphs that name the same numbers
- report regression, survival, and diagnostic-accuracy results correctly
- avoid the common statistical reporting errors, multiplicity included
:::

The methods section and results section are a contract. The methods announce, in advance, every analysis you will report; the results deliver them, in the same order, with the same terminology. A results section that contains analyses not named in the methods is unreported work. A methods section that names analyses absent from the results is unfulfilled specification. Reviewers read both against each other, and mismatches are one of the most common reasons for major revisions.

This chapter provides worked templates for the most common analytical scenarios in clinical health research. Each template pairs a methods paragraph with its results paragraph, because the two must be read and written as a unit. The SAMPL guidelines [@lang2015sampl] catalogue the minimum statistical information that must appear in any biomedical article; this chapter operationalises that catalogue as paired paragraphs you can adapt directly.

## The vocabulary rule

Name the analysis once in methods, using the exact term you will use in results. If the methods say *"multivariable logistic regression"*, the results say *"in multivariable logistic regression"* — not *"in the adjusted model"* or *"after controlling for covariates"*, which are vague and inconsistent. If methods name five covariates, results use the same five, in the same order. Adding or silently dropping a covariate between sections is an inconsistency that reviewers catch and that readers cannot resolve without contacting the authors.

## Multivariable regression

**In methods:**

> *"The association between NT-proBNP at discharge and 30-day readmission was assessed using multivariable logistic regression. Covariates were selected a priori based on clinical relevance and included age, sex, NYHA class at admission, and LVEF measured during the index hospitalisation. Effect modification by LVEF was assessed with a multiplicative interaction term. Model discrimination was quantified by the c-statistic with 95% CI by the DeLong method [@delong1988roc]."*

**In results:**

> *"After adjustment for age, sex, NYHA class, and LVEF, NT-proBNP at discharge was independently associated with 30-day readmission (adjusted OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.08–1.59, p = 0.005). There was no evidence of effect modification by LVEF (interaction p = 0.42). Model discrimination was moderate (c-statistic 0.71, 95% CI 0.68–0.74)."*

Three things in this results paragraph. The effect estimate appears as OR + 95% CI + p-value in a single parenthetical. The interaction test is reported even when non-significant, because it was named in methods. The c-statistic is reported with its own CI, not as a bare number.

## Survival analysis

Most survival analyses in clinical research involve three related outputs reported across two to three sentences: the event rate, the Kaplan-Meier comparison, and the Cox regression estimate. Write them in that order.

**In methods:**

> *"Time to 30-day readmission was analysed using Kaplan-Meier estimation, with group comparisons by the log-rank test. The independent association between NT-proBNP at discharge and time to readmission was assessed with a Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for the same covariates as the logistic regression. NT-proBNP was modelled both continuously (per log-unit increment) and in quartiles. The proportional hazards assumption was examined by Schoenfeld residuals [@schoenfeld1982residuals]."*

**In results:**

> *"The 30-day readmission rate was 12.8% (95% CI 11.9–13.7%). Kaplan-Meier curves showed a higher cumulative incidence of readmission in patients with NT-proBNP ≥ 1,000 pg/mL at discharge (log-rank p < 0.001; Figure 2). In multivariable Cox regression, NT-proBNP at discharge was independently associated with time to readmission both continuously (adjusted HR per log-unit: 1.31, 95% CI 1.08–1.59, p = 0.005) and across quartiles, with a monotonic gradient from Q1 (reference) to Q4 (adjusted HR 2.14, 95% CI 1.56–2.94). The proportional hazards assumption was satisfied for all covariates (global Schoenfeld test p = 0.61)."*

The order matters: event rate first, visual result second, adjusted estimate third. The Schoenfeld test is reported regardless of the result; it was named in methods.

## Diagnostic accuracy

Diagnostic accuracy studies produce a cluster of statistics that should be reported together: AUC, threshold, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. Predictive values depend on prevalence, which must be stated explicitly so readers in different settings can reinterpret them.

**In methods:**

> *"The discriminative ability of NT-proBNP at discharge for 30-day readmission was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. The AUC with 95% CI was calculated by the DeLong method [@delong1988roc]. The threshold associated with the maximum Youden index [@youden1950index] was identified and used to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and positive and negative predictive values with 95% Wilson confidence intervals [@wilson1927interval]."*

**In results:**

> *"The AUC for NT-proBNP at discharge was 0.71 (95% CI 0.68–0.74). At the threshold of 1,000 pg/mL (Youden index 0.31), sensitivity was 73% (95% CI 69–77%) and specificity 62% (95% CI 61–64%). Given the observed readmission prevalence of 12.8%, the positive predictive value was 21% (95% CI 19–24%) and the negative predictive value 94% (95% CI 93–95%)."*

## The missing-data paragraph

Missing-data handling requires two coordinated paragraphs: one in methods (what you planned) and one in results (what you found and whether it mattered). They must name the same numbers and be consistent in terminology.

**In methods:**

> *"NT-proBNP at discharge was available for 5,065 of 5,204 participants (97.3%). For all covariates, missingness was below 2%. Complete-case analysis was the primary approach. A pre-specified sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation by chained equations [@vanbuuren2011mice] (20 imputed datasets; predictive mean matching for continuous variables, logistic regression for binary variables) was conducted to assess the influence of missing data on the primary result [@sterne2009missing]."*

**In results:**

> *"The complete-case analysis included 5,065 participants. In the multiple imputation sensitivity analysis, results were consistent with the primary analysis: the adjusted OR was 1.28 (95% CI 1.05–1.56) in the imputed dataset, compared with 1.31 (95% CI 1.08–1.59) in the complete-case analysis."*

Note what this results paragraph does not say: it does not declare the results "similar" without a number. It reports both estimates in the same format and lets the reader judge.

## Sensitivity analyses

Name each sensitivity analysis in methods and give it a label — (i), (ii), (iii) or a short descriptor — that you will repeat exactly in results.

**In methods:**

> *"Three pre-specified sensitivity analyses were conducted: (i) restricting to patients with LVEF < 50%; (ii) excluding patients with a prior HF admission in the preceding 12 months; (iii) replacing NT-proBNP with BNP as the exposure, available in a subset of 2,068 patients."*

**In results:**

> *"In sensitivity analysis (i), restricted to patients with LVEF < 50% (n = 2,410), the adjusted OR was 1.38 (95% CI 1.08–1.77). In analysis (ii), after excluding patients with prior HF admission (n = 3,687), the adjusted OR was 1.29 (95% CI 1.02–1.63). In analysis (iii), BNP was associated with readmission in the subset (adjusted OR 1.26, 95% CI 0.99–1.59, p = 0.06). The primary result was consistent across analyses (i) and (ii); analysis (iii) was underpowered to confirm the association."*

The labels (i), (ii), (iii) match the methods exactly. Each estimate is reported in the same format as the primary result. The last sentence gives an honest summary that distinguishes which analyses were consistent and which were not, and why.

## Non-significant pre-specified primary outcome

A null result for a pre-specified primary endpoint must be reported as a result, not as a failure. Do not frame it as "the study was underpowered" unless post-hoc power analysis was pre-specified; the methods should have included a power calculation, and if that calculation was adequate the null result stands.

**In methods:**

> *"The primary outcome was the proportion of patients with NT-proBNP below 1,000 pg/mL at six months. Based on a pilot study estimating a 45% responder rate in the control arm, 600 participants (150 per arm) provided 80% power to detect a 15 percentage-point absolute difference at a two-sided α of 0.05."*

**In results:**

> *"The proportion with NT-proBNP below 1,000 pg/mL at six months did not differ significantly across treatment arms (ACEi 48%, ARB 46%, CCB 43%, Placebo 44%; χ² test p = 0.61). The absolute difference between the most effective arm (ACEi) and placebo was 4 percentage points (95% CI −4 to 12 pp). The study was adequately powered to detect a 15 percentage-point difference; the observed difference was smaller than the pre-specified minimum clinically important difference."*

Two things this results paragraph does: reports the data with a 95% CI on the difference (not just a p-value), and states the power argument in terms of the pre-specified minimum detectable effect rather than claiming underpowering.

## Discordant sensitivity analysis

When a sensitivity analysis produces a different result from the primary analysis, report both, note the direction of the discordance, and interpret it in terms of what changed. Do not bury the difference, and do not over-interpret it as contradicting the primary result unless the sensitivity analysis was pre-specified to do so.

**In methods:**

> *"A pre-specified sensitivity analysis repeated the primary logistic regression in the sub-cohort of patients with index NT-proBNP above the study median (≥ 1,500 pg/mL; n = 2,540), in whom the association was hypothesised to be stronger."*

**In results:**

> *"In the full cohort, NT-proBNP at discharge was associated with 30-day readmission (adjusted OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.08–1.59). In the pre-specified sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with index NT-proBNP ≥ 1,500 pg/mL, the adjusted OR was 1.09 (95% CI 0.83–1.43), with the confidence interval crossing the null. This attenuation is consistent with the higher baseline readmission rate in this subgroup reducing the relative discriminative contribution of discharge NT-proBNP; it does not contradict the primary finding but limits its extension to the highest-risk stratum."*

The last sentence does the interpretive work: it explains the mechanism of the discordance rather than simply noting it.

## Common statistical reporting errors

The templates above are about reporting an analysis correctly. A separate discipline is avoiding the errors that survive peer review most often. Five recur.

**Multiplicity.** Test twenty independent hypotheses at α = 0.05 and, on average, one comes up "significant" by chance alone. A paper that runs many comparisons and reports the significant ones without adjustment is fishing. State how many tests were planned and correct for them: Bonferroni for a small confirmatory family, Benjamini–Hochberg (false-discovery rate) for a large exploratory screen [@bender2001multiple]. A single pre-specified primary outcome needs no correction — but then say so, rather than leaving the reader to count.

**Subgroup fishing.** A subgroup effect that was not pre-specified, was tested as one of many, and is reported because it reached significance is a hypothesis, not a finding. Report the pre-specified subgroups, test for interaction rather than comparing within-subgroup p-values, and label any post-hoc subgroup as exploratory (open science chapter). "The drug worked in diabetics," pulled from an unplanned split of an otherwise null trial, is the canonical way to mislead.

**P-value misuse.** A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and "non-significant" is not "no effect" (Chapter: presenting data). Report the estimate and its confidence interval first; the p-value is a footnote to the effect size, never a substitute for it. Never write `p = 0.000`, and never use `NS` in place of a number.

**Correlation and causation.** An association from observational data is not a causal effect, however carefully adjusted. Reserve causal verbs (*reduces*, *causes*, *leads to*) for randomised evidence or an explicit causal-inference design; use associational language (*was associated with*) otherwise, and name residual confounding as a limitation (Chapter: clear writing, on hedging).

**Overfitting.** A model tuned until it fits the data at hand will not fit the next dataset. Discrimination measured on the same data used to build the model is optimistic; report validated performance and calibration, not apparent performance ([prediction models](prediction-models.qmd)).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Practice: find the mismatch

The methods and results paragraphs below contain three inconsistencies. Identify each one.

**Methods:** *"The association between discharge NT-proBNP and 30-day readmission was assessed by multivariable logistic regression, adjusted for age, sex, NYHA class, LVEF, and eGFR. A sensitivity analysis excluding patients with atrial fibrillation was pre-specified."*

**Results:** *"After adjustment for age, sex, LVEF, and renal function, the adjusted OR was 1.31 (95% CI 1.08–1.59). The finding was consistent in the sensitivity analysis excluding patients with prior heart failure admission."*

---

Answers:

1. Methods names eGFR as a covariate; results substitutes *"renal function"* — an inconsistent term.
2. Methods names NYHA class as a covariate; results drops it from the adjustment list without explanation.
3. The pre-specified sensitivity analysis excluded patients with atrial fibrillation; the reported sensitivity analysis excluded patients with prior heart failure admission — a different criterion entirely.
:::
